name: uncover
purpose: Unified CLI that queries multiple internet-scan databases (Shodan, Censys, FOFA, Hunter, ZoomEye, Netlas and others) with one syntax and returns matching hosts.
journalism_use_case: Find exposed servers, cameras or admin panels tied to an entity under investigation across several scan databases with one query — the practical route from 'this company sells interception gear' to 'these are its internet-facing systems and certificates'.
pros: One query syntax across many scan vendors removes a real friction: each vendor's query language differs and comparing results by hand is error-prone
Multiple sources mitigate single-vendor coverage gaps, which are substantial and uneven by region
MIT, single Go binary, very actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-17) with only 6 open issues
Pairs naturally with certificate-transparency and ASN work to build an infrastructure picture of a vendor or state agency
cons: Requires API keys for Shodan, Censys, FOFA, Hunter, ZoomEye and similar — several of which are paid, so the capability has a real recurring cost that the free tool hides

Your queries and target identifiers are sent to commercial scan vendors, who therefore learn exactly which organisations you are investigating — a serious operational-security consideration when the target is a surveillance company
Infrastructure focus only: it maps hosts, not people or social activity
Scan-database results are snapshots that can be months stale, so a host appearing or disappearing is weak evidence without corroboration
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 3,120 stars with 6 open issues and same-day pushes (2026-11-17), release v1.2.1 (2026-05-20). ProjectDiscovery maintains a well-known suite of such tools with consistent release discipline.
assessment: Valuable for surveillance-industry investigation, with the privacy trade-off stated plainly: you are telling a commercial scan vendor which companies you are looking at. For your profile I would use a dedicated account and egress not linked to the newsroom's main identity, prefer Metabigor's keyless sources for the first pass, and reserve uncover for when you need depth. Verify any host attribution against RIR and certificate data before publishing.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.2.1 (2026-05-20), 3,120 stars, 6 open issues. Same-day commits with a very clean tracker under an organisation that maintains a consistent tool suite.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — the scan data belongs to the respective vendors under their terms.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. The binding constraints are each scan vendor's API terms, which typically restrict redistribution of their data — relevant if you want to publish a dataset derived from their results.
costs: Software free. Real cost is the API keys: Shodan, Censys, FOFA, Hunter and ZoomEye each have free tiers with tight quotas and paid tiers above them — current prices not verified in this survey (check each vendor). Budget for at least one paid subscription if this is a regular workflow.
privacy: Your queries and target identifiers are sent to commercial scan vendors. This is the weakest point: investigating a surveillance vendor while telling a scan provider exactly who you are looking at is a genuine exposure. Use separated accounts and egress.
alternatives: Metabigor for keyless public-source footprinting first
Direct certificate-transparency queries (certstream, crt.sh) which disclose less
amass for subdomain enumeration from your own vantage point
blockers: Queries disclose your investigation targets to commercial scan vendors; several required APIs are paid

name: Zoekplaatje
purpose: Firefox extension that records the search-engine results pages a user visits — result order, snippets, ads, timestamps — and exports them as structured data for analysis.
journalism_use_case: Document what a search engine actually showed, when, and in what order — the evidence base for algorithmic-bias, search-manipulation and disinformation-ranking stories, where the claim is about the ranking itself and a screenshot is not enough.
pros: Captures ranking order and snippet text as structured data, which is precisely the artefact an algorithmic-accountability story needs and which no screenshot provides
Data stays local in the browser and is exported by the user, so the capture process itself leaks nothing
Built by a research group with a methodological track record in platform studies, so the data model is designed for analysis rather than display
Still receiving commits (pushed 2026-11-17), unusual longevity for a research extension
cons: Very small user base (14 stars) and Firefox-only, so it is a specialist instrument rather than general tooling
Engine coverage is limited to implemented parsers, and engines change their markup frequently — a parser that silently stops matching produces empty captures
Manual: someone must actually perform the searches, so systematic comparison across accounts, locations or times requires disciplined protocol design by you
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION despite MPL-2.0, so compliance records need the file reference
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 14 stars means there is no community signal to report. Documented: MPL-2.0 with SPDX NOASSERTION, release v1.12 (2026-01-23), last push 2026-11-17. DMI tools are used in academic platform research, which is relevant adjacent credibility.
assessment: A narrow instrument that is close to irreplaceable when your story is about search ranking. For your profile the methodological work matters more than the tool: define the protocol (which queries, from which accounts, locations and times) before collecting, because the finding lives or dies on comparability. Verify the parser is capturing before running a campaign — a silent parser failure would waste the whole collection.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.12 (2026-01-23), SPDX NOASSERTION (MPL-2.0 per repository), 14 stars, 8 open issues. Same-day commits from an institutional research group; tiny community but current maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured SERP content belongs to the engines and publishers.
licence_restrictions: MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft on modifications. Capturing SERPs may engage engine terms of service — a separate question from the licence, and worth considering before a large collection campaign.
costs: No fee. No infrastructure. Cost is analyst time performing searches.
privacy: Captured SERP data is stored locally in the browser and exported by the user — nothing is uploaded. Note that the searches themselves are visible to the engines in the normal way, so the search campaign has a visible footprint even if the capture does not.
alternatives: 4CAT for broader platform data collection and analysis
shot-scraper for scripted screenshot evidence of SERPs (weaker as structured data)
Manual screenshots plus a disciplined logging spreadsheet for very small studies

name: name-variant-search
purpose: Browser-based tool that generates transliteration and spelling variants of a personal name across scripts and conventions, producing a list of alternative spellings to search for.
journalism_use_case: Expand searches for a person whose name is transliterated inconsistently across Russian, Ukrainian, Arabic or other scripts — the difference between finding three records and finding thirty, and a routine failure point in cross-border investigation.
pros: Addresses a specific, high-frequency failure in cross-border research that reporters usually handle badly by guessing a couple of spellings
Runs client-side in a hosted static page, so the name you enter is not transmitted — a genuinely important property when the name is a sensitive subject
Built by Bellingcat for practising investigators, so the variant conventions reflect real research needs rather than linguistic completeness
MIT licensed and trivial to self-host as a static page if you prefer not to rely on the hosted version
cons: Heuristic variant generation only: it produces candidate spellings, not a verified list, and will both miss real variants and generate spellings nobody uses
No search execution or results — you take the list elsewhere, so it is one step in a manual workflow
Small project (56 stars, 2 open issues) with no releases and last push 2026-06-25
Variant quality depends on the source script and convention; coverage for less common scripts was not evaluated in this survey
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 56 stars, 2 open issues, no releases, last push 2026-06-25, MIT licence. Bellingcat's tool suite is widely used in the investigative community, which is relevant context rather than specific evidence for this tool.
assessment: A small, sharp utility worth having bookmarked and worth self-hosting as a static page so you are not dependent on the hosted copy. For your profile the correct use is to feed its output into a systematic search across SearXNG, Marginalia and your own document archive, keeping a record of which spellings were searched — because 'we searched for the name' is a weak methodological claim and 'we searched these fourteen transliterations' is a strong one.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-06-25, no releases or tags, 56 stars, 2 open issues. Five months quiet on a small static tool that is functionally complete; low risk from dormancy since there is no dependency surface to rot.
costs: No fee. No infrastructure; self-hosting is a static file.
privacy: Name input is processed client-side in the hosted static page, so the name is not transmitted to a server. Self-hosting removes even the page-load disclosure to the hosting provider.
alternatives: uroman for systematic romanisation in a pipeline rather than interactively
rigour for corporate rather than personal name normalisation
Manual transliteration tables for a specific language pair where precision matters

name: OSINT Framework
purpose: Interactive tree-structured directory of OSINT resources and tools organised by the identifier or artefact you start from — username, email, domain, phone number, image.
journalism_use_case: Starting point for choosing a collection method or source type when you know the identifier you hold but not the tooling — a reporter with a phone number and no idea what can be done with it finds the categories of approach in a minute.
pros: The 'start from the identifier you hold' structure matches how an investigation actually begins, which is why it remains the most-used orientation resource in this field (12,467 stars)
Broad coverage across identifier types, including categories a newcomer would not think to look for
MIT licensed and self-hostable as a static site, so you can fork and prune it into a newsroom-specific version
Still maintained (pushed 2026-10-31), unusual for a link directory of this age
cons: A directory, not a tool: it tells you what exists, not whether it works, and link quality and freshness vary widely — several categories point to dead or hostile services
No maintenance or trust signalling on entries, so a reporter cannot tell a maintained tool from an abandoned one or a data broker from a research resource
194 open issues, many of them link-rot and submission requests, indicating curation lags submissions
Linking out to third-party services means following a link can disclose your interest to a commercial data broker — a risk a newcomer will not anticipate
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 12,467 stars with 194 open issues, last push 2026-10-31, no releases. The large open-issue count on a link directory is itself evidence of curation lag.
assessment: Useful for orientation and actively harmful if used uncritically, because it does not distinguish a maintained open tool from a paid people-search broker that will log your query. For your profile the valuable move is to fork it, strip the categories you will never use and the services you consider unsafe, and keep an internal version with your own trust annotations. Use this catalogue's assessments for anything you intend to deploy.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-31, no releases, 12,467 stars, 194 open issues. Episodic curation updates with a large pending backlog; the project is alive but curation does not keep pace with link rot.
licence_restrictions: None. Forking and pruning is explicitly easy under MIT, which is the recommended use.
costs: No fee. Many linked services are paid or freemium, and their costs are not catalogued — a hidden cost of following the tree.
privacy: No investigative data flows of its own; it is a link index. The risk is downstream: linked third-party services, including commercial people-search brokers, will see your queries and may retain them. Brief reporters before pointing them at it.
alternatives: This catalogue for maintenance- and licence-verified assessments
Bellingcat's online investigation toolkit for a curated, practitioner-maintained list
A pruned internal fork with trust annotations

name: CouncilSearcher
purpose: Tool that searches across UK and Ireland local-council meeting records and transcripts for keywords or named individuals.
journalism_use_case: Local-government accountability reporting: find what a named councillor actually said about an issue across many meeting transcripts — work that otherwise means opening dozens of PDFs on dozens of council websites.
pros: Targets a genuinely under-served area: local-government records are where accountability journalism has thinned most, and they are fragmented across hundreds of sites
Cross-council search is the specific capability that makes a pattern story possible ('fourteen councils discussed the same contractor')
MIT licensed, small and readable, so adapting the approach to another jurisdiction is feasible
Built by Bellingcat with practising investigators in mind
cons: Scoped to UK and Ireland, so it is irrelevant outside those jurisdictions and the code would need real work to generalise
Small project with light maintenance: 17 stars, 7 open issues, last push 2026-01-07 — ten months before this survey
Depends on council websites and transcript sources whose structures change, so coverage will silently degrade
No releases, so there is no version to pin
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 17 stars means there is minimal community signal. Documented: last push 2026-01-07, 7 open issues, no releases, MIT licence.
assessment: Relevant only if your work touches UK or Irish local government, in which case it is worth trying despite light maintenance — the alternative is manual PDF trawling. The more generalisable value for your profile is the pattern: a cross-jurisdiction transcript index is a high-value, low-glamour capability, and building one for the jurisdictions you cover (using Scrapy for collection and Datasette or Solr for search) is a realistic project with a clear accountability payoff.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-01-07, no releases, 17 stars, 7 open issues. Ten months without activity on a tool whose data sources (council websites) change continuously — for a scraper-dependent project this is a material decline signal rather than benign stability.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Council records are public documents subject to the relevant jurisdiction's terms.
costs: No fee. Minimal compute; storage for fetched records.
privacy: Fetches public council records to local storage. Your requests are visible to the council websites, which is unremarkable for public records.
alternatives: Scrapy plus Datasette to build an equivalent index for your own jurisdictions
mySociety tooling (TheyWorkForYou, Alaveteli) for UK parliamentary and FOI material
Manual search for a one-off question about a single council
blockers: UK/Ireland only; scraper-dependent with ten months of no maintenance

name: katana
purpose: Fast Go web crawler with both standard and headless (Chromium) modes, JavaScript parsing, form filling and configurable scope, outputting discovered URLs and endpoints.
journalism_use_case: Enumerate every reachable page and document on a target site — PDFs, archives, staging paths, orphaned directories — before mirroring or analysis. This is how you find the procurement annex nobody linked from the navigation.
pros: Headless mode parses JavaScript to find endpoints that static crawlers miss, which matters on modern government portals built as single-page applications
Fast and scope-configurable, so you can crawl a large site without accidentally crawling the internet
MIT, single Go binary, very actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-17) with an exceptionally clean tracker (28 open against 17,862 stars)
Composes well: pipe its output into a WARC capture tool or a document downloader
cons: Discovers URLs rather than preserving content, so it must be paired with a capture tool for anything evidentiary — an easy step to forget
Crawling from your own host makes a visible request pattern to the target, and an aggressive crawl can be mistaken for an attack or trigger blocking
Form filling and headless crawling can have side effects on poorly built sites (triggering submissions, consuming resources) — real care is needed on live government systems
Security-tooling heritage means defaults are tuned for penetration testing rather than polite journalism; rate limits need setting deliberately
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 17,862 stars with 28 open issues and same-day commits (2026-11-17), release v1.8.0 (2026-10-05). ProjectDiscovery's suite has consistent release discipline, verifiable across its repositories.
assessment: The right discovery tool for a target site, used with explicit politeness settings. For your profile the workflow I would standardise: katana to enumerate, a filter for document extensions, then browsertrix-crawler or wget --warc to capture the documents you want as evidence. Set rate limits and disable form interaction on live public-service sites — a crawl that degrades a council's website is both an ethical and a legal problem, and it will end the access.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.8.0 (2026-10-05), 17,862 stars, 28 open issues. Same-day commits, regular releases, very low backlog relative to adoption.
licence_restrictions: None material for the code. Crawling engages the target's terms of service and, in some jurisdictions, computer-misuse law if done aggressively — a legal rather than licence consideration.
costs: No fee. Chromium for headless mode adds resource use. Negligible infrastructure.
privacy: Direct HTTP(S) requests from your host to the target, so the target sees your IP and request pattern. For a sensitive target, crawl from a dedicated egress rather than the newsroom's address.
alternatives: Photon for a lighter Python crawler focused on harvesting contacts and links
Scrapy when you need structured extraction rather than URL discovery
browsertrix-crawler when capture fidelity rather than enumeration is the goal

name: Scrapy
purpose: Mature Python framework for building web crawlers that extract structured data, with built-in request scheduling, throttling, retry handling, item pipelines and export formats.
journalism_use_case: Build repeatable bulk collection of structured public records — court listings, corporate registries, planning applications, classifieds — into datasets for analysis. This is the workhorse behind most data-journalism collection that is not a one-off script.
pros: Handles the unglamorous parts properly: politeness delays, retries, deduplication, concurrency limits and resumable crawls — the things ad-hoc scripts get wrong and that determine whether a multi-day collection completes
Enormous ecosystem and the best documentation in this category, so a new engineer can be productive in a day and the code is maintainable by the next person
BSD-3-Clause and very actively maintained (release 2.20.0 on 2026-11-06, 65,442 stars) with a long track record of stability
Item pipelines give you a clean place to validate and normalise records at collection time, which materially improves dataset quality
cons: Developer tool: no UI, no archiving or evidentiary output by default, so a Scrapy dataset is analysis input rather than evidence of what a page said
No JavaScript rendering natively — dynamic sites need scrapy-playwright or a separate headless step, which adds complexity
Learning the framework's conventions (spiders, items, middlewares) is an upfront cost that a simple requests script avoids for small jobs
176 open issues; large-site crawls still require hand-tuning of throttling to avoid blocking or harming the target
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey, but Scrapy's use in data journalism is extensively documented in the field's teaching materials and in newsroom open-source repositories (openstates-scrapers, querido-diario and similar projects are Scrapy-based, which is verifiable from those repositories).
assessment: Adopt as the standard for any collection you expect to run more than once. For your profile the decisive feature is resumability and throttling: a registry crawl that takes four days and can be paused is the difference between a dataset and a failed attempt. Always add a separate evidentiary capture for the specific pages a story will cite — Scrapy gives you data, not proof of what was published.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 2.20.0 (2026-11-06), 65,442 stars, 176 open issues. Regular releases over more than a decade with commercial backing (Zyte) and a broad contributor base.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Collected content belongs to the source publishers.
licence_restrictions: None material for the framework. Scraping engages target sites' terms and, for personal data, data-protection law — both separate from the licence and both real considerations for a registry crawl.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: a VM for long crawls; optional paid proxy or headless-browser services if the target blocks you (vendor costs not priced here). Engineer time is the main cost.
privacy: Requests go from your infrastructure to the targets, and data is stored locally. The target sees your IP and pattern. For personal data in registries, your own data-protection obligations attach to the collected dataset — treat it as regulated material, not just files.
alternatives: Crawlee for a JavaScript/TypeScript-native equivalent with browser support built in
katana for URL discovery rather than structured extraction
requests plus BeautifulSoup for genuinely one-off small jobs

name: Crawlee
purpose: Node.js and Python crawling library with unified HTTP and browser (Playwright/Puppeteer) crawlers, automatic request queueing, proxy rotation, session management and anti-blocking features.
journalism_use_case: Collect JavaScript-heavy public pages — dynamic dashboards, infinite-scroll listings, map-based registries — that simple HTTP crawlers cannot render. For a TypeScript-centric newsroom stack it is the natural collection layer.
pros: Browser and HTTP crawling behind one API, with automatic fallback, so you do not maintain two codebases for static and dynamic targets
Session and proxy management is built in, which is what makes sustained collection from blocking-prone targets practical
Apache-2.0, very actively maintained (pushed 2026-11-17, v4.0.0-rc.2 in progress, 26,475 stars) with a clean tracker
Native TypeScript support means it fits a modern newsroom web stack without a language switch
cons: Engineering-heavy with no investigative UI or evidence packaging — same gap as Scrapy
Optional paid proxy providers and the Apify cloud platform are the vendor's commercial path; using them means proxy vendors see your target URLs, a disclosure worth weighing
Node/browser resource footprint is heavier than Scrapy's for equivalent static crawling
Rapid major-version movement (4.0 release candidates) means pinning and migration planning are necessary
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 26,475 stars with 145 open issues, release v3.18.2 (2026-09-29) with v4.0.0-rc.2 tagged, same-day pushes. Commercially backed by Apify, whose business model is the hosted platform — which explains both the strong maintenance and the pull toward paid services.
assessment: The right choice if your stack is TypeScript or if the targets are genuinely dynamic; Scrapy remains better for large static collection with a Python team. For your profile the thing to watch is the commercial gravity: the anti-blocking story leads naturally to paid proxies, and routing an investigation's target URLs through a proxy vendor is a disclosure. Self-host the egress where the targets are sensitive.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v3.18.2 (2026-09-29), tag v4.0.0-rc.2, 26,475 stars, 145 open issues. Same-day commits, active major-version development, commercial backing.
licence_restrictions: None material for the library. The Apify platform and paid proxy services operate under their own commercial terms.
costs: Library free. Optional paid dependencies are the real cost driver: proxy providers and the Apify cloud are usage-priced (rates not verified in this survey). Self-hosted browser crawling needs more CPU and RAM than HTTP crawling — budget accordingly.
privacy: Target requests go via your host or, if configured, third-party proxies — in which case the proxy vendor sees the target URLs and timing. That is a meaningful disclosure for a sensitive investigation and should be a deliberate choice.
alternatives: Scrapy for Python teams and large static crawls
katana for enumeration rather than extraction
Playwright directly for a handful of dynamic pages where a framework is overkill

name: HTTrack
purpose: Website copier that recursively downloads a site to a local directory tree, rewriting links so the copy is browsable offline.
journalism_use_case: Take a quick offline mirror of a site likely to be edited or taken down, for later reading and keyword search — the low-ceremony option when a page is about to disappear and you need a copy now, on a machine with no Python or Docker.
pros: Extremely easy to run with a GUI and a CLI, available packaged in most distributions, and still releasing (3.51.0, 2026-10-28) after decades
No dependencies of consequence, so it works on a borrowed or locked-down machine where installing a toolchain is not possible
Produces a browsable, grep-able file tree, which is immediately useful for reading and keyword search without replay infrastructure
Astonishingly clean issue tracker (5 open against 4,844 stars) for a project of this age
cons: Produces a loose file tree, not WARC, so it is weak as evidence of record: no HTTP headers, no request/response fidelity, no capture provenance — a mirror can be edited afterwards and nothing in it proves otherwise
Poor with dynamic and JavaScript-dependent sites, which describes most modern government portals — you will get shells
Link rewriting alters the content, which is itself a problem for evidentiary use
Aggressive defaults can hammer a target; rate limiting must be set deliberately
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 4,844 stars with 5 open issues and a release on 2026-10-28, pushed 2026-11-17 — an exceptionally well-kept long-lived project. Its weakness relative to WARC-based capture is a general property of mirroring, widely discussed in web-archiving practice.
assessment: Keep it for the convenience case and do not use it as your evidence path. For your profile the rule is simple: HTTrack for reading and searching a site offline, WARC-based capture (browsertrix-crawler, Scoop, wget --warc) for anything that may be cited or disputed. Its enduring value is deployability — when a reporter abroad needs a copy of a site in the next ten minutes on an unfamiliar laptop, this is what will work.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 3.51.0 (2026-10-28), 4,844 stars, 5 open issues. Current releases and near-zero backlog after many years; a mature tool under continuing care.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Mirrored content belongs to the original publisher.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the software. Mirroring engages the target's terms of service and copyright in the mirrored material — relevant if you redistribute the mirror rather than using it internally.
costs: No fee. Disk proportional to site size. Negligible.
privacy: Direct downloads from the target to local disk, so the target sees your IP and a heavy request pattern. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler or wget --warc for evidentiary WARC capture
monolith or SingleFile for single-page portable snapshots
grab-site for steerable rapid-response archiving — but note its maintenance status
blockers: Not WARC: weak provenance, unsuitable as evidence of record
